Paragraphs: Tamacahut n wuccen d yizem
The Tale of the Wolf and the Lion
Tigi d timucuha n wedrar n Ǧeṛǧeṛ, adrar aberkan, adrar n nnif, adrar n lḥif: akken i s‑yenna win n zzman:

''W'ibɣan lḥeṛma ad tagar''
''Yali s adrar,''
''Yečč abelluḍ bu tcacit;''
''W'ibɣan irden n tfazit''
''Iṣubb s azaɣar:''
''Ad yeɣleb agdi d temrit!''
Yura‑tent ccix Yebṛahim Asedqaw di ttnaṣfa n lqern ṛbeɛṭac, ad yessifes fell‑as Ṛebbi di ddunit, yeɛfu fell‑as di laxeṛt! Amin!
These are the tales of the mountain of Djurdjura, the black mountain, the mountain of honor, the mountain of hardship; as the ancient one used to say:

''Whosoever desires that honor should prevail''
''Let him ascend the mountain,''
''And feed upon the capped acorn;''
''Whosoever desires the pure wheat''
''Let him descend into the plain:''
''He shall be more abused than a hound!''
Written by Sheikh Ibrahim of the Ait Sedqa towards the middle of the fourteenth century, may God lighten his burdens in this world, and grant him forgiveness in the afterlife! Amen!

Source.Title: Leǧmeɛ n lewḥuc
Paragraphs: Di zzman amezwaru, nnejmɛen lewḥuc, akken llan, myeɛhaden s Ṛebbi ur myuččen, ad hennin di ddunit. Semman izem d agellid fell‑asen (ay d agellid, ɣas Ṛebbi!), rṣan tilas d inagan.

Izem yezdeɣ di teẓgi d tameqqrant, netta d wuccen d yilef d tewtult d weɣyul d tyaziṭ d tfunast, llan d lxeddam‑is, f wakken d‑ssawalen tamacahut. Mkul axeddim iqeṭṭu‑yas ṣṣalḥa: ilef, yeggan fell‑as; uccen, yeddal yiss: tawtult, yessummut‑itt; abareɣ yettagem‑as‑d aman; aɣyul izeddem‑as‑d isɣaren; tayaziṭ tettarew‑as‑d timellalin: tafunast tettak‑as‑d ayefki.
Hennan lewḥuc: teksa taɣaṭ d wuccen! Feṛḥen, aɛlaxaṭer lehna yeḍmen leɣna.

Lḥaṣul, ṣeggmen ddunit lukan ur asen‑tt‑yessexṣer ara wuccen yerra yizem d amṛayi. Uccen ur yefṛiḥ ara s uṣeggem agi n ddunit: yuɣ tannumi yekkat timeɣriwin; yendem f liḥala taqdimt: mi d‑yesmekti aksum azegzaw d idammen yeḥman, ad as‑yuɣal d tisselbi. Ass‑a ḥeṛmen: acu ara yili w'ixedmen? Ad yeɛṣu? Accaren n yizem qeḍɛen, lḥekm‑is akken nniḍen. Ihi, ijebd‑d taḥṛaymit, yessefra ad yessefreɣ di lxeddam n yizem s tuffra yiwen yiwen, ad yuɣal d imciṭni.

Translation.Title: The Assembly of the Animals
Paragraphs: In ancient times, the animals gathered together, all of them, and swore by God not to devour one another, so that they could live in peace in the world. They appointed the lion as king over them (though God is the only true King!), and they established borders and covenants.

The lion lived in a vast forest, and the wolf, the boar, the hare, the donkey, the hen, and the cow were his servants, according to how the story is told. To each servant, he assigned a specific task: the boar, he slept upon him; the wolf, he covered himself with him; the hare, he used her as a pillow; the fox fetched water for him; the donkey gathered firewood for him; the hen laid eggs for him; and the cow gave him milk.
The animals lived in peace: the goat grazed alongside the wolf! They rejoiced, because peace guarantees prosperity.

In short, they arranged the world beautifully, if only the wolf—whom the lion had made his advisor—had not ruined it for them. The wolf did not rejoice in this harmony of the world: he was accustomed to causing chaos; he regretted the old state of affairs. When he remembered fresh meat and warm blood, which were now forbidden, it drove him to madness. What was to be done? Should he disobey? The lion's claws were sharp, and his rule was absolute. Therefore, he resorted to cunning, plotting in secret to incite the lion's servants, one by one, to rebellion, turning into a true demon.

Source.Title: Lmux n ubaṛeɣ
Paragraphs: Uccen iḥili yettkel yerna lxeddam irkel kkes abareɣ, mmi‑s n ɛemmi‑s. Abareɣ yuki d wuccen d lexṛaza‑s, yebna f yiman‑is. Lameɛna, ayen yebɣa Ṛebbi ad yeḍru: urant.
Yiwwass, yuḍen yizem aṭṭan afessas: yewt‑it ubeḥri. Yečča timellalin di ticcent; armi ur d‑yefki ara Ṛebbi tawwurt, yesnejmeɛ‑d lxeddam irkel, icaweṛ‑iten.

Mkul yiwen d aḥeckul d‑yerna.
Yenna‑yas ubareɣ:
‑ Ttcekkiṛen idammen n wuccen: qqaren d ddwa ameqqran.
Yexẓer yizem Si Mḥemmed… ffɣen ddaw‑as.
‑ Iǧaweb‑d wuccen: D ṣṣeḥḥ, a lmir n lewḥuc, lameɛna ma xelṭen di lmux n ubareɣ.

Iwwet yizem abareɣ, iɣḍel‑d lmux‑is yemmut. Yejreḥ wuccen iman‑is ljerḥ ameẓyan, yesquddeṛ‑d kra idammen, xedmen ddwa i lmir n lewḥuc. Yenna‑yas yizem:
‑ Ddem, a Ben Yeɛqub, ad tneṭleḍ!
Yewwi wuccen abareɣ armi d targa, yečč‑it: yenṭel kan taglimt d yeɣsan. Yefṛeḥ, yenna deg wul‑is: Tura, ur yelli wugur wala aɛekkeṛ.

Translation.Title: The Brain of the Fox
Paragraphs: The wolf was confident he was the most cunning among all the servants except for the fox, his cousin. The fox was well aware of the wolf and his trickery, and he stood on his guard. However, what God wills must happen: it was written.
One day, the lion fell ill with a mild ailment: he had caught a cold. He ate eggs with garlic; but since God did not yet grant a recovery, he gathered all the servants together and consulted them.

Everyone suggested a different remedy.
The fox said:
‑ People praise the blood of the wolf: they say it is a great medicine.
The lion glared at Sir Mḥemmed… and the wolf soiled himself out of fear.
‑ The wolf replied: It is true, O ruler of the animals, but only if it is mixed with the brain of the fox.

The lion struck the fox, smashing his skull, and he died. The wolf inflicted a small wound upon himself, drawing a few drops of blood, and they prepared the medicine for the ruler of the animals. The lion said to him:
‑ Take him, O Ben Yeɛqub, and bury him!
The wolf carried the fox away as far as the ditch and devoured him: he buried only the skin and the bones. Rejoicing, he said in his heart: Now, there is no longer any obstacle or hindrance.

Source.Title: Uccen d tewtult
Paragraphs: Tusa‑d tefsut: tezzegzew tmurt, teǧǧuǧǧeg, fsant ttjuṛ, ttarwen lewḥuc.

Iṛuḥ wuccen yewt‑as llir i tewtult, yenna‑yas:
‑ Yessetma‑m, aha‑tent sɛant‑d arraw nsent: ad ten‑awint i tzirit ad jellben di leḥcic, ad ččen zzeɛteṛ neɣ isegmi ufeqqus. Kem, qqim dagi ad kem yessummut lmir n lewḥuc!
Ur as‑d‑terri tewtult d aɛṛab wala d aqbayli, lameɛna tegr‑d tinexsas: nnḍen‑as lehduṛ n wuccen i wul‑is, am cečči, qebren‑tt.

Ɛeddan kra n wussan, tuɣal tuɣ awal n wuccen: tṛuḥ s izem, tenna‑yas s tergigit:
‑ A lmir n lewḥuc, ad iyi‑tserrḥeḍ: bɣiɣ ad ṛuḥeɣ: ɛyiɣ!
Yeɛreḍ yizem ad tt‑id‑yeṭṭef, ad tt‑id‑yerr s abrid: iḥawet, yessaged, ur yufi. Teɛṣa‑t: abaden! Yewt‑itt. yerẓa‑tt: yenna‑yas:
‑ Ddem, a Ben Yeɛqub, ad tneṭleḍ!
Yewwi‑tt wuccen, yečča‑tt, yemceḥ idammen: yefṛeḥ, iǧeɛl ussan yelhan qrib ad d‑uɣalen.

Translation.Title: The Wolf and the Hare
Paragraphs: Spring arrived: the earth turned green, the flowers bloomed, the trees budded, and the animals gave birth to their young.

The wolf went and spoke enticingly to the hare, saying to her:
‑ Look at your sisters, they have already given birth to their little ones: they take them out under the full moon to leap about in the grass, eating thyme or the shoots of melons. As for you, you stay here just to be used as a pillow by the ruler of the animals!
The hare answered him neither in Arabic nor in Kabyle, but she sighed deeply: the words of the wolf wrapped around her heart like a poison, consuming her inside.

A few days passed, and she followed the wolf's words: she went to the lion and said to him, trembling:
‑ O ruler of the animals, set me free: I want to leave; I am exhausted!
The lion tried to hold her back, to bring her back to her senses: he reasoned with her, he threatened her, but to no avail. She defied him completely! So he struck her, crushing her, and said to him:
‑ Take her, O Ben Yeɛqub, and bury her!
The wolf carried her away, devoured her, and wiped away the blood: he rejoiced, believing that the good old days were soon about to return.

Source.Title: Uccen d tyaziṭ
Paragraphs:
Iɛedda wayen iɛeddan, iṛuḥ wuccen ɣer tyaziṭ, yewt‑as izli n tyaziḍin, yenna‑yas:
‑ A weltma, d acu kem‑yeǧǧan dagi? Izem, mi d‑turweḍ tamellalt, yečč‑itt, talli timital‑im zedlent; mi ssefṛuṛxent, ffɣen‑d yefṛax, ad ten‑sḍefṛent tyemmatin tiseɛdiyin s iguduyen d tmizar d tebḥirin, nitni d ibaḥanen irkel d ičuččiwen irkel; mi ɛyan di tikli d wexbaḍ d tyessawt, neɣ yenɣa‑ten usemmiḍ, ad ten‑jemɛent seddu wafriwen‑nsent iwakken ad ḥmun steɛfun; ad imɣurent, ffɣent‑d irkel d tifṛax d sut tcebbubin!

Tayaziṭ ur as‑t‑id‑terri imiren merreɣ wala messus, lameɛna tegr‑d tinexsas: yesxeṣr‑as nneyya. Teqqim kra n wussan, tuɣal awal n wuccen, tṛuḥ s izem, tenna‑yas:
‑ A lmir n lewḥuc, serreḥ‑iyi ad ṛuḥeɣ: ɛyiɣ!
Yeɛreḍ yizem ad tt‑id‑yeṭṭef, ad tt‑id‑yerr s abrid: iḥawet, yessaged: ur yufi, Tugi: abaden! Yewt‑itt, yerẓa‑tt. Yenna‑yas:
‑ Ddem, a Ben Yeɛqub, ad tt‑tneṭleḍ!

Yewwi‑tt wuccen, yečča‑tt, yerna yemceḥ idammen.
Yefṛeḥ, yenna deg wul‑is: Ussan yelhan qerben!

Translation.Title: The Wolf and the Hen
Paragraphs:
Time passed, and the wolf went to the hen, sang her the song of hens, and said to her:
— My sister, what has left you here? The lion, when you lay an egg, eats it, while your peers are brooding; when they hatch, and the chicks come out, the blessed mothers will guide them through the dungheaps, the gardens, and the orchards, all of them beautiful and chirping; when they are tired of walking, scratching, and guarding, or if the cold hurts them, they gather them under their wings so they can warm up and rest; they will grow up, and they will all turn into young pullets with crests!

The hen did not return an answer to him at that moment, neither bitter nor sweet, but she sighed: he had shaken her good faith. She stayed for a few days, then turned back to the wolf's words, went to the lion, and said to him:
— O king of the animals, allow me to leave: I am tired!
The lion tried to catch her, to bring her back to the path: he coaxed, he threatened: he found no way. She refused: never! He struck her and broke her. He said:
— Take her, Ben Yeɛqub, and go bury her!
The wolf took her away, ate her, and wiped the blood. He was joyful and said in his heart: The good days are near!

Source.Title: Uccen d weɣyul
Paragraphs:
Imiren yebren wuccen s aɣyul, d nnuba‑s. Yenna‑yas:
‑ Atma‑k, a bu imeẓẓuɣen, ha‑ten deg wegdal, di leḥcic ar tɛebbuṭ, ṛwan asennan d umezzir, la ttejɛun, kkaten tuqqra, yiwen ur asen‑yettalas. Keč, qqim dagi ad txedmeḍ tacemlit.

Akken yesla weɣyul i imeslayen agi, yebra i imeẓẓuɣen‑is, yegr‑d tinexsas. Yiwen n yiḍ, s udem n ṣṣbeḥ, yurga yewwi‑yas‑d Ṛebbi yella deg wegdal netta d weɣyul nniḍen, la ttemyekmazen tuyat, Yefṛeḥ, yendekwal‑d seg yiḍes, yufa‑d iman‑is weḥd‑s: tuɣal ddunit deg wul‑is d alili.

Iṛuḥ s izem, yenna‑yas:
‑ A lmir n lewḥuc, serreḥ‑iyi ad ṛuḥeɣ: ɛyiɣ!
Yeɛreḍ yizem ad t‑id‑yerr s abrid, ur yufi: aɣyul, ma ifat yeḥṛen, yekfa umeslay. Yewt‑it, yerẓa‑t, yenna‑yas:
‑ Ddem, a Ben Yeɛqub, ad tneṭleḍ!
Yeskerker‑it wuccen armi d iɣẓer, yeqqim‑as yečča deg‑s geddac n wussan.

Asmi i d‑yuɣal, yenna‑yas yizem:
‑ Annaɣ, a Mḥemmed, teǧǧiḍ‑aɣ i fad!
Yuɣ lḥal d uccen i d‑yettagmen. Yerra‑yas:
‑ A lmir n lewḥuc, armi d ass‑agi ay kfiɣ tanṭelt n wehdum nni: mi neṭleɣ fettus, iḍehṛ‑d qejjiṛ; mi neṭleɣ qejjiṛ, iḍehṛ‑d fettus!

Translation.Title: The Wolf and the Donkey
Paragraphs:
Then the wolf turned his attention to the donkey; it was his turn. He said to him:
— Your brothers, O long‑eared one, look at them in the meadow, with grass up to their bellies, sated on thistle and lavender, growing fat and kicking up their heels, and no one has a claim over them. You, you stay here to do the Drudgery.

As soon as the donkey heard these words, he let down his ears and sighed. One night, towards the break of dawn, he dreamed that God had placed him in the meadow, he and another donkey, scratching each other's shoulders. Overjoyed, he woke up with a start from his sleep and found himself all alone: the world turned as bitter as oleander in his heart.

He went to the lion and said to him:
— O king of the animals, allow me to leave: I am tired!
The lion tried to bring him back to the path, but found no way: once a donkey becomes stubborn, talking is over. He struck him and broke him, then said:
— Take him, Ben Yeɛqub, and go bury him!
The wolf dragged him all the way to the ravine, settled down, and fed on him for several days.

When he returned, the lion said to him:
— Hey, Mḥemmed, you have left us to die of thirst!
For it was the wolf who used to fetch the water. He replied to him:
— O king of the animals, only today have I finished burying that carcass: whenever I buried a front hoof, a hind leg appeared; and whenever I buried a hind leg, a front hoof appeared!

Source.Title: Uccen d yilef
Paragraphs:
Seg weɣyul, uccen yeɛna ilef. Yenna‑yas:
‑ Atma‑k, ha‑ten la ẓẓaden abelluḍ, ttfeggilen akal s temɣilin‑nsen ssekfalen abeɛɛuq d iɛemmuṛen. Mi ṛwan, ṛuḥen ṭṭsen deg segnan‑nsen, cexxṛen, yiwen ur asen‑yettalas. Keč. tuɣaleḍ‑as dagi d tagertilt i yizem! Yernu, tḥesbeḍ iman‑ik d bab n yiɣil!

Ixaq yilef, Yecxeṛ fell‑as; yerwel. Iṛuḥ wuccen s izem, yenna‑yas:
‑ A lmir n lewḥuc, qareɛ iman‑ik: ufiɣ‑n ilef la yesseqḍaɛ timɣilin‑is, yettgalla deg‑k!
Yenna‑yas yizem:
‑ Amek ara t‑ɛeqleɣ ad iyi‑d‑yebdu?
Yenna‑yas wuccen:
‑ Mi twalaḍ anyir‑is yekres, bnu f yiman‑ik! (ɣas ar anyir n yilef dayem ikerres!)
Yebren s ilef, yenna‑yas:
‑ Ɛass iman‑ik: la yettgalla deg‑k yizem!
Yenna‑yas yilef:
‑ Amek ara t‑ɛeqleɣ ad iyi‑d‑yebdu?
Yenna‑yas wuccen:
‑ Mi twalaḍ cclaɣem‑is la reqqsen, bnu f yiman‑ik! (ɣas ar cclaɣem n yizem dayem reqqsen!)
Wwḍen tameddit, yemmuqel yizem deg yilef, iwala anyir‑is yekres; yemmuquel yilef deg yizem, yufa cclaɣem‑is la reqqsen. Msemlalen s temɣilin d waccaren, yiwen la iṛeɛɛed, wayeḍ la icexxeṛ.

Uccen ineggez akkin, ar as‑yeqqar:
‑ A tiḥeddiṛt ḥedṛeɣ ass‑a!… A dda izem! A dda ilef!…
Yewt‑it yizem, yerẓa‑t. Uccen yezla‑t, iselx‑it, igezm‑it d sslayeɛ, ččan seg‑s geddac d tiremt. Yefṛeḥ wuccen, yenna deg wul‑is: Ussan yelhan uɣalen‑d!

Translation.Title: The Wolf and the Boar
Paragraphs:
After the donkey, the wolf turned his attention to the boar. He said to him:
‑ Your brothers, look at them, they are grinding acorns, digging up the earth with their tusks, and unearthing heaps of starchy tubers. When they are full, they go to sleep in their wallows, snoring, and no one dares to challenge them. But you, you have become like a floor mat for the lion here! And yet, you consider yourself a master of strength!

The boar grew anxious and snorted with anger at him; the wolf fled. The wolf then went to the lion and said to him:
‑ O king of the animals, protect yourself: I found the boar sharpening his tusks and swearing against you!
The lion said to him:
‑ How will I recognize that he is about to attack me?
The wolf replied:
‑ When you see his brow furrowed, prepare yourself! (Even though the brow of a boar is always furrowed!)
He then turned back to the boar and said to him:
‑ Watch yourself: the lion is swearing against you!
The boar asked him:
‑ How will I recognize that he is about to attack me?
The wolf replied:
‑ When you see his whiskers twitching, prepare yourself! (Even though the whiskers of a lion are always twitching!)

When evening arrived, the lion looked at the boar and saw that his brow was furrowed; the boar looked at the lion and found that his whiskers were twitching. They clashed with tusks and claws, one roaring and the other snorting.

The wolf leaped aside, shouting:
‑ O what a disaster I am witnessing today!… O Uncle Lion! O Uncle Boar!…

The lion struck him and broke his back. The wolf slaughtered him, skinned him, cut him into quarters, and they ate several meals from him. The wolf rejoiced and said in his heart: The good days have returned!

Source.Title: Uccen d tfunast
Paragraphs:
Teqqim‑d tfunast, yeɛreḍ wuccen ad tt‑yessinef: ulac lḥila ur as‑d‑yejbid ara, ulac tamacahut ur as‑d‑yewwi ara; tugi ad teɛṣu: abaden!
Tenna‑yas: Tiẓgi tettɛici‑yi: izem yewqem lḥeṛma i teẓgi: sumeḥɣ‑as ayefki‑w seg wul zeddigen am waman.

Yuɣal wuccen yebren s izem, ar as‑yekkat di tfunast: yugi yizem ad as‑yessemḥes. Yenna‑yas:
‑ Ḥesbeɣ‑tt am yemma: ad fell‑as yeɛfu Ṛebbi!
Iɛewweq wuccen, yessusem.

Lḥan ayen lḥan, yuɣal‑it, yenna‑yas:
‑ A lmir n lewḥuc, d ṣṣeḥ, tafunast ur k‑teɛṣi ara, lameɛna ur tezmir ara ad k‑tɛic: keččini, mačči, d llufan ad tidireḍ s uyefki; yernu, lmir n lewḥuc, ur as‑d‑tewwi ara ad yuɣal d ameksa neɣ ad t‑ineɣ laẓ. Ma yewweḍ akken ara tellaẓeḍ, qebleɣ ad iyi‑teččeḍ nekkini s yiman‑iw: tura lewḥuc ɛṣan‑k, leɛhed irreẓ, amek ara tɛiceḍ? Yessefk‑ak ad tseggdeḍ, neɣ ad k‑ineɣ laẓ. Mačči d aksum n tfunast ideg iyi‑teḥṣel lmeɛna, d aglim‑is: yenna‑yi wemɣar azemni, xeddmen seg‑s ticifaḍ d lɛali‑tent: mi tent‑telsiḍ, mačči d tikli ara telḥuḍ neɣ d tazzla ara tazzleḍ: d affug ara tafgeḍ! Ad teṭṭilliḍ i iseddilen d iɣeẓran: ulac lweḥc ur tettaṭṭafeḍ ara deg umecwaṛ: ad ak‑tuɣal ṣṣyada d tteqṣir.
Ma d ṛṛay‑iw, yessefk tafunast ad temmet aksum‑is ad teṭṭfeḍ yess taṛwiḥt, si maḍil ara ifeṛṛeǧ Ṛebbi; aglim‑is, ad ak‑ṣenɛeɣ seg‑s ticifaḍ.
Yeqbel yizem, nnig wul: nɣan tafunast, selxen‑tt, ččan‑tt kra kra, ffren aglim‑is.

Translation.Title: The Wolf and the Cow
Paragraphs:
The cow remained, and the wolf tried to turn her away: there was no trick he did not pull on her, and no story he did not bring her; she refused to disobey: never!
She said to him: The forest sustains me: the lion has established respect for the forest: I grant him my milk from a pure heart, like water.

Then the wolf turned to the lion, striking against the cow: the lion refused to listen to him. He said to him:
‑ I consider her like my mother: may her soul rest in peace!
Perplexed, the wolf fell silent.

They went on for some time, then he returned to him and said:
‑ O king of the animals, it is true, the cow did not disobey you, but she cannot sustain you: you yourself are not a baby to live on milk; furthermore, for the king of the animals, it is not fitting to become a herder or to let hunger kill him. If it comes to the point where you starve, I accept that you eat me, my very self: now the animals have disobeyed you, the pact is broken, how will you live? You must hunt, or hunger will kill you. It is not the meat of the cow that catches my attention, it is her hide: a wise old man told me that they make excellent shoes from it: when you wear them, it is not walking that you will walk or running that you will run: it is flying that you will fly! You will look down upon the thickets and the ravins: there is no beast you will not catch in a short distance: hunting will become a pastime for you.
If it is my advice, the cow must die so you can sustain your soul with her meat, until God brings relief; as for her hide, I will craft the shoes for you out of it.
The lion accepted, against his heart: they killed the cow, skinned her, ate her bit by bit, and hid her hide.

Source.Title: Ticifaḍ n wuccen
Paragraphs: Yewweḍ‑d unebdu, yuẓa‑d uɣamac. Imelleḥ wuccen aglim n tfunast, idhen‑it, ifser‑it i tili iwakken ad yeqqar s lɛql‑is.

Asmi yewǧed, igzem‑it d isriḥen d tyigiwin, yextaṛ seg‑sent snat n lɛali i yizem. iqass‑as‑tent, armi d‑ṣebḥent, yebda lexṛaza: mi d‑yewwi seg weglim n tfunast, yernu‑d seg weglim n yizem, ixiḍ tindict: mkul nnefda, ad isuɣ yizem, ad as‑yini wuccen:
‑ Akken qerrḥent ay neffɛent!
Ixerreẓ di tcifaḍ agi si ṣṣbeḥ armi d azal: yiwen yettsuɣu, wayeḍ yeqqar‑as:
‑ Akken qerrḥent ay neffɛent!

Imiren yewwi‑t armi d yiwet n tiɣilt nnig yefri d ameqran, yerra‑t tinnegnit, yenna‑yas:
‑ Mekken iḍarren‑ik i ṛebɛa i yiṭij: alamma qqurent tcifaḍ ara lhunt.

Yeqqim din yizem i yiṭij n ssmayem armi d tizwa: ssewwen iḍarren‑is: yeqqur fell‑asen weglim. Tekka fell‑as tkeffaṛt. Uccen iqubel‑it‑id i tili si lbeɛd. Mi d‑yebda ubeḥri, yessawel‑as, yenna‑yas:
‑ Neggez tura: ad teẓreḍ ma ur tettafgeḍ ara am wefṛux deg genni!

Ineggez yizem di lkaf, yegrareb f qerru f iḍarren armi d lqaɛa n yeɣẓer: yeqtel irkel: ula d addud ur yezmir ara ad ibedd. Uccen yendi‑yas‑tt ad t‑ineɣ, ad t‑yečč ula d netta, armi i t‑iwala yemneɛ, yerwel.

S udem n tmeddit, a‑t‑a lferg usekkur yuɣ‑d iɣẓer d tasawent, yufa‑d izem di yir lḥala.
Nnant‑as tsekkrin:
‑ Ɛahed‑aɣ s Ṛebbi ur aɣ‑teččiḍ, ad k‑nsellek!

Iɛahed‑itent. Uɣalent ar d‑ttawint aman deg qubab‑nsent, slexsent ticifaḍ armi yerḍeb weglim; xesfent‑d lexyuḍ, ɣlint tcifaḍ, Yemmeɣ yizem s leḥṛaṛa f tsekkurt, yessebleɛ‑itt: yerẓa leɛhud n Ṛebbi. Yuɣal ifa: tufeg‑d tedder seg uɛebbuḍ‑is!
Yekker yizem la ileḥḥu inedder armi d lɣar‑is, yeṭṭes: ur as‑yexdim ara waṭṭan annect i s‑yexdem wurrif.

Translation.Title: The Shoes Crafted by the Wolf
Paragraphs: Summer had arrived; the heat became oppressive. The wolf salted the cow's hide, oiled it, and spread it out in the shade so that it would dry slowly.

When it was ready, he cut it into strips and sections; he chose two of the best pieces for the lion. He fitted them to him, and once they were properly sized, he began his cobbling: for every stitch, he passed the needle through the hide of the cow and then through the skin of the lion. Each time the needle pierced, the lion would roar, and the wolf would tell him:
‑ The more they hurt, the more good they do!
He cobbled away at these shoes from morning until noon: one was roaring, and the other was saying:
‑ The more they hurt, the more good they do!

Then he led him to a knoll just above a great cave, made him lie on his back, and said to him:
‑ Direct your four feet toward the sun: the shoes will not be ready until they are dry.

The lion remained there under the midsummer sun until the afternoon breeze: his feet were burning hot, and the hide dried and tightened upon them. He suffered agonizing pain. The wolf faced him from afar, watching from the shade. When the breeze picked up, he called out to him and said:
‑ Jump now! You will see if you do not fly like a bird in the sky!

The lion jumped into the cliff and tumbled head over heels down to the bottom of the ravine: he was completely broken, and he could not even stand up. The wolf had set this trap for him to kill him so that he could eat him too, but when he saw that he survived, he fled.

Toward evening, a covey of partridges moved up the ravine and found the lion in a terrible state.
The partridges said to him:
‑ Swear to us by God that you will not eat us, and we will save you!

He made the pact with them. They began bringing water in their beaks, soaking the shoes until the leather softened; they cut away the threads, and the shoes fell off. Filled with fierce hunger, the lion pounced upon a partridge and swallowed her whole: he broke his oath to God. Then he gaped, and she flew out alive from his stomach!
The lion got up and went groaning back to his cave, where he lay down: he did not suffer from his injuries as much as he suffered from his rage.

Source.Title: Ttaṛ n yizem
Paragraphs: Yeḥbes yizem geddac n wussan di lɣar‑is; uɣalen iḍarren‑is ibezgen ṭṭreḍqen d arṣeḍ, teǧǧa‑t tawla i t‑yettaɣen seg‑sen.
Mi d‑yesmekti taḍsa yeḍsa fell‑as wuccen, d lexdiɛa i t‑yexdeɛ, ad iṛɛed am tegnewt.

Asmi ccwi, yekker yeffeɣ ad iqelleb f wuccen, ad d‑yerr ttaṛ‑is. Yetti‑d fell‑as ddunit d wi tt‑yuman, ur t‑yufi.
Yiwwass, yessemlal‑iten Ṛebbi deg wemḍiq: ssya u ssya, d lḥiḍ n weẓru iṣeggem am trigla. Uccen, tekfa fell‑as ddunit: iwala lmut teḥdeṛ‑d: tusa‑d mm lḥeq!

Yewt‑it yizem am falku, izgel‑it: igzem‑as kan ajeḥniḍ!
Uccen cṭir, terna‑yas tugdi lxaffa: yuli deg weẓru am wemcic di lḥiḍ. Yewweḍ ɣer lemneɛ, nnug wemḍiq, yeqqim din: qquren ifadden‑is, la yettergigi am yifer.

Yesxenzer yizem ajeḥniḍ n wuccen s wuglan‑is d waccaren‑is armi ineẓ‑d ur yeddi d gma‑s, yuɣal yenna‑yas:
‑ A Mḥemmed, ay axeddeɛ, cfu f imeslayen‑iw, tgeḍ leqrar i yiman‑ik! Tikelt agi zegleɣ‑k, temneɛḍ‑iyi, lameɛna ɛllmeɣ‑k: anda telliḍ ad k‑ɛeqleɣ ger watma‑k: ɣas ad teqqim ddunit yiwwass, ad k‑ṭṭfeɣ, ad k‑rẓeɣ deg uzagur, ur tettnejbaṛeḍ ara: ad ččeɣ lmux‑ik, sweɣ idammen‑ik!
Ssyen, mkul yiwen yuɣ abrid‑is.

Translation.Title: The Vengeance of the Lion
Paragraphs: The lion stayed inside his cave for many days; his feet became swollen and burst with suppuration, and the fever that caught him from them left him helpless.
When he remembered the laugh the wolf had laughed at him, and the betrayal he had betrayed him with, he would thunder like a storm cloud.

When he felt slightly better, he rose and went out to search for the wolf, to take his revenge. He turned the world upside down and looked everywhere, but he did not find him. One day, God brought them together in a place: from this side and that side, it was a wall of rock straight as a snare. For the wolf, the world came to an end: he saw death present before him: the owner of justice had arrived!

The lion struck at him like a falcon and missed him: he only cut off his tail! The wolf was clever, and fear added to his swiftness: he climbed up the rock like a cat on a wall. He reached safety, out of reach, and sat there: his limbs stiffened, and he was shaking like a leaf.

The lion tore the wolf's tail with his teeth and his claws until it was shredded completely, then he turned and said to him:
— Oh Mḥemmed, you betrayer, remember my words, you have sealed your own fate! This time I missed you and you escaped me, but I warn you: wherever you are, I will recognize you among your brothers. Even if the world has only one day left, I will catch you, I will break your backbone so you will never be mended: I will eat your brains and drink your blood!
From then on, each one took his own path.

Source.Title: Tameɣrust n "ḥdeṛ bbwa"
Paragraphs: Seg wasmi i s‑yettwagzem ujeḥniḍ, ur ihenna wuccen: ikcem‑it ttexmim d uḥebbeṛ. Seg wakken iɛewweq amek ara yexdem, iṛuḥ s amɣer azemni ad t‑id‑iciweṛ. Yefka‑yas‑d asɣar n tmeɣrust yeqqur, yerna iḍebber fell‑as.

Yewwi‑t wuccen, yeẓẓa‑t di tniri. Deg yiwet n teswiɛt, yezzegzew, fetḥen lɛiwen‑is, fkan‑d iferrawen, ṣeggmen ifurkawen, yuɣal d taneqlett. Ssyen, tefruri tazart, wwant tbexsisin, la d‑ɣellin iniɣman ileqqaqen ur yelli d lweqt‑nsen.

Imiren yendeh wuccen f watmaten‑is, usan‑d irkel, tɛeǧǧben: tameɣrust n Belɛejjuḍ tewwa! Bdan la tetten tazart taleqqaqt, ttnaɣen. Yenna‑yasen Mḥemmed:
‑ Ay atmaten, annect agi d leqbiḥ, yecmet!
Yuɣal, iwakken ad d‑ters leqniɛa deg wulawen‑nsen, yernu mkul yiwen ad yečč leḥq‑is, icadd‑asen irkel tiɣaṭṭwin s wemrar ɣer lǧedra n tmeɣrust, imiren ihuzz‑itt, tuɣal tazart am wakal di lqaɛa.
Uccanen la tetten, mkul yiwen iqeddem tirni‑s, netta yeqqim‑asen‑d d aɛessas f yiwet n tiɣilt tqureb‑iten‑id.

Akken iwala lhan d cceɣl‑nsen, stamnen, yebda ar yekkat yettsuɣu:
‑ Uccayen! Imnayen! A Ben Yeɛqub, a‑ten‑ayen!
Mxeṛwaɛen wuccanen, jebden rewlen, mkul yiwen d abrid i t‑yefkan, ǧǧan irkel tiɣaṭṭwin‑nsen deg wemrar.
Yefṛeḥ Mḥemmed: ayen yebɣa yewweḍ ɣur‑s: tura uccanen irkel ur sɛin ara ijeḥnaḍ: ulamek i t‑yeɛqel yizem gar‑asen!

Translation.Title: The Fig Tree of "Watch out for it!"
Paragraphs: From the day his tail was cut off, the wolf was never at peace: worry and anxiety entered him. Because he was so confused about what to do, he went to an ancient elder to consult him. The elder gave him a dry cutting of a fig tree and advised him on what to do.

The wolf took it and planted it in the desert plain. In an instant, it turned green, its buds opened, it put forth leaves, its branches formed, and it became a young fig tree. Then, the figs hatched, the early figs ripened, and the soft, sweet fruits began to fall before their season.

Right away, the wolf called out to his brothers; they all came and were amazed: the marvelous fig tree was ripe! They began to eat the soft figs and fight each other. Mḥemmed said to them:
— Oh brothers, this behavior is wicked and ugly!

Then, so that contentment would settle in their hearts and each one would eat his fair share, he tied all of their tails with a rope to the trunk of the fig tree. Then, he shook it, and the figs became like dust on the ground.
The wolves ate, each advancing in his own row, while he stood watch over them from a nearby hill.

As soon as he saw they were fully occupied and felt safe, he began to strike and shout:
— The hounds! The horsemen! Oh Ben Yeɛqub, there they are!
The wolves panicked, pulled with all their might, and fled, each taking whichever path opened before them, leaving all of their tails behind in the rope.
Mḥemmed rejoiced: he had achieved what he wanted. Now, all of the wolves had no tails: there was no way for the lion to recognize him among them!

Source.Title: Tibḥrt n lebṣel
Paragraphs:
Yiwwass, yeffeɣ yizem ad iṣegged, yemmuger yiwen n wuccen yettwagzem‑as ujeḥniḍ. Yewt‑it, yerẓa‑t, yečča lmux‑is, yessegra idammen‑is: iɣil yenɣa aɛdaw‑is.
Azekka nni, yemlal‑d d wuccen nniḍen yettwagzem‑as ula d netta ujeḥniḍ.
Yewhem wayrad: yeṭṭef‑it, yesteqsa‑t, yeḥka‑yas‑d tamsalt n tmeɣrust n "ḥdeṛ bbawa"; isserreḥ‑as, iṛuḥ.

Seg wakken iɛewweq yizem amek ara yexdem, iṛuḥ s amɣar azemni ad t‑id‑iciwer, ad iḍebber fell‑as. Yenna‑yas:
‑ Ṛuḥ, xdem tibḥirt n lebṣel aqerḥan, tawiḍ ɣur‑s uccanen irkel ad t‑ɣeẓẓen: a win d‑yennan: ḥ ḥ ḥ! d win ay d axṣim‑ik!

Iṛuḥ yizem yekrez taɣzut kamel s waccaren‑is, yeẓẓa‑tt d lebṣel, iketteṛ deg‑s urḍan. Ur teqqim ara tebḥirt tezzegzew am lebḥeṛ. Imiren, yendeh f wuccanen, usan‑d irkel. Ye deg‑sen ad t‑ɣeẓẓen, ur d‑yettɣimi yifer wala tabellust. Yenna‑yasen:
Win ara d‑yinin: ḥ ḥ ḥ! ad t‑ččeɣ, ṣṣeḥḥa u ṣṣlaḥ, lqewwa u ccbeḥ!

Bdan wuccanen la ɛeddren; yiwen ur d‑yenni: ḥ ḥ ḥ!… Ḥaca axṣim n yizem, lameɛna yetḥeṛma: iwakken ad yekkes zzeɛf, mi iɣeẓẓa cwiṭ, yin'as:
‑ Niɣ, a sidi, tenniḍ win ara d‑yinin: ḥ ḥ ḥ! ad t‑ččeɣ, ṣṣeḥḥḥa u ṣṣlaḥḥḥ, lqewwa u ccbeḥḥḥ!
Yin'as yizem:
‑ Swa‑swa!
Ad yernu cwiṭ ad yenṭeq s uccanen:
‑ Teslam, ay atmaten? Iɛeggen‑awen lmir n lewḥuc ɣur‑wat ad tettum: win ara d‑yinin: ḥ ḥ ḥ! ad t‑yečč, ṣṣeḥḥḥa u ṣṣlaḥḥḥ, lqewwa u ccbeḥḥḥ!
Ad as‑inin:
‑ Swa‑swa!
Akkenni, armi yekfa lebṣel, ur d‑teqqim tbellust wala ifer, izem ur yefhim ara, axṣim ur d‑iban ara.

Translation.Title: The Onion Garden
Paragraphs: One day, the lion went out to hunt and met a wolf whose tail was cut off. He struck him, broke him, ate his brains, and licked up his blood; he believed he had killed his enemy. The next day, he met another wolf who also had his tail cut off.
The lion was amazed: he caught him and questioned him, and the wolf told him the story of the "Watch out for it!" fig tree; he let him go, and the wolf left.

Because the lion was so confused about what to do, he went to the ancient elder to consult him and ask for his advice. The elder said to him:
— Go, make a garden of very sharp onions, and bring all the wolves there to chew them up. Whoever says: ḥ ḥ ḥ!, that one is your enemy!

The lion went and plowed a whole fertile valley entirely with his claws, planted it with onions, and watered it heavily. Before long, the garden turned green like the sea. Then, he called out to the wolves, and they all came. He coerced them to chew them all up, so that not a single leaf or bulb would remain. He said to them:
— Whoever says: ḥ ḥ ḥ!, I will eat him, health and heartiness, strength and handsomeness!

The wolves began to crunch; not one of them said: ḥ ḥ ḥ!... except the lion's enemy. However, he was clever: to relieve his burning mouth, whenever he chewed a little, he would say to him:
— Is it not so, my lord, that you said whoever says: ḥ ḥ ḥ! you will eat him, ḥ‑ḥ‑ḥ‑health and ḥ‑ḥ‑ḥ‑heartiness, strength and ḥ‑ḥ‑ḥ‑handsomeness!
The lion replied to him:
— Exactly!
Then he would turn to the other wolves and speak after chewing a bit more:
— Did you hear, my brothers? The king of the animals has warned you, watch out lest you forget: whoever says: ḥ ḥ ḥ!, he will eat him, ḥ‑ḥ‑ḥ‑health and ḥ‑ḥ‑ḥ‑heartiness, strength and ḥ‑ḥ‑ḥ‑handsomeness!
They would answer him:
— Exactly!
In this way, until the onions were completely gone and not a bulb or a leaf remained, the lion did not understand the trick, and his enemy was never found out.

Source.Title: Lmut n wuccanen
Paragraphs: Iwala yizem ad as‑yemneɛ Mḥemmed, ur d‑yetterra ara seg‑s ttaṛ.
Yuɣal yendi‑yasen i wuccanen ad mmten irkel, ad yettekki wexṣim‑is.
Iṣubb‑iten s asif. Uccanen, yeččuṛ uɛebbuḍ‑nsen d lebṣel aqerḥan: tekker tmes di tyersi d iẓerman‑nsen. Ye deg‑sen ad swen asif kamel, ad t‑ḥebsen, mačči ad tɛeddi tiqit.
Bdan la tessen armi ɛellelen, ṭṭemblen iɛebbaḍ‑nsen seg waman d lebṣel, la snukkufen: Ḥebsen ur zmiren ad rnun wala ad rewlen. Mḥemmed ifhem‑itt: isers kan imi‑s f waman, ur yenṭerr ara.

Ssyen, inheṛ‑iten wayrad armi d ifri nni deg yegrareb.
Ye deg‑sen ad neggzen: d lmut qbala, lameɛna, izem, d ayen ugaden i‑yebɣa: iḥreṣ‑iten: bdan ar ttneggizen. Mi ineggez yiwen, seg‑sen, yegrireb deg yefri, teṭṭerḍeq tɛebbuṭ‑is, yemmet, ineggez wayeḍ, yegrireb, yemmet am umezwaru armi i d‑yeqqim Mḥemmed d aneggaru. Ijelleb deg yefri, yerwel, yemneɛ: armi d imiren i t‑yeɛqel yizem.
Yebren lmir n lewḥuc ɣer lɣar‑is, ur t‑yewwi igenni, ur t‑tewwi tmurt: la iṛeɛɛed si zzeɛf, terna‑yas nndama imi yenɣa uccanen irkel baṭel.

Translation.Title: The Death of the Wolves
Paragraphs: The lion saw that Mḥemmed would escape him, and that he would not take his revenge upon him.
He turned to trap all the wolves so they would all die, so that his enemy would be included among them.

He brought them down to the river. The wolves, their bellies were full of sharp, pungent onions: fire had ignited in their throats and their intestines. He coerced them to drink the entire river, to stop its flow, so that not a single drop would pass.

They began to drink until they choked, their bellies bloated from the water and the onions, and they gasped for breath: they stopped, unable to add another drop or to flee. Mḥemmed understood it: he simply placed his mouth on the water and suffered no harm.

After that, the lion drove them like cattle to that precipice down which he had rolled. He coerced them to jump: it was certain death, but what they feared was exactly what the lion desired: he pressed them, and they began to jump. When one of them leaped, he rolled down the precipice, his belly burst, and he died; another jumped, rolled down, and died just like the first one, until Mḥemmed was left as the last. He bounded into the precipice, fled, and escaped: only then did the lion recognize him.
The king of animals turned back to his cave, neither the sky nor the earth could hold him: he was thundering with rage, compounded by the regret of having killed all the wolves in vain.

Source.Title: Aṭṭan n yizem
Paragraphs: Yesteɛmel yizem men yuɣ yuɣ dayen, ur as‑teḥṣil ara lmeɛna deg wuccen. Ur iqelleb fell‑as, ur yesteqsa deg‑s geddac. Yebɣa ad t‑iwet di laman.
Asmi iǧeɛl yettu lḥal, isers‑d f yiman‑is aṭṭan ameqran, la yettergigi, inedder.

Iceggeɛ ɣer lewḥuc ad d‑asen, ad mmeẓren, ad msamaḥen. Umnen lewḥuc: usan‑d. A win ikecmen ɣer lɣar‑is, ad t‑id‑iẓer, yečč‑it; a win ikecmen ɣer lɣar‑is, ad t‑id‑iẓer, yečč‑it! Ula d yiwen ur d‑yeffiɣ d ssalem!

Yusa‑d ula d uccen. Yessawel‑as si beṛṛa, yenna‑yas:
‑ A lmir n lewḥuc, amek telliḍ?

Iɛeql‑it‑id yizem, yeldi‑d allen‑is, yufa‑t yebɛed, Yuɣal ar d‑yettru amzun tewweḍ‑it‑id mm lḥeq:
‑ Kecm‑d, a Mḥemmed, ad nemsamaḥ! Nek, a‑tt‑a teṛwiḥt di lfawatt!

Yugi wuccen, yerra‑yas:
‑ Ad nemsamaḥ kan ssya. Ḥareɣ: ɣur‑i ccɣel!

Armi i t‑id‑yeḥṛes yizem, yenna‑yas:
‑ Ala lǧeṛṛa uṣubbu ay ufiɣ, tin n tuɣalin, ulac!

Iṛɛed yizem am tegnewt, yenna‑yas:
‑ Ad k‑ineɛl Ṛebbi, ay axeddeɛ! A cciṭan yerẓan leɛhud n Ṛebbi! Ad ig Ṛebbi ddnub n widen irkel deg tsewwqeḍ armi ten‑nɣiɣ ad ak‑ɛellqen i yiri weḥd‑k ass n lḥisab d lɛiqab! Seg wass‑a d tasawent, nek yid‑k, taɛdawt terṣa; seg wass‑a d tasawent, ger dderya‑w d dderya‑k, taɛdawt terṣa alamma tenger ddunit!
Ssyen, mkul yiwen yuɣ abrid‑is.
Mazal ar ass‑a, taɛdawt terṣa ger yezmawen d wuccanen.

Mi k‑tuɣ deg yiḍ di lexla, uccanen la neṭṭqen neɣ sekkren timeḥbibert, fhem belli bu tissas ulaḥed‑it di tmurt nni; ma temsusam ddunit, ur la neṭṭqen ara wuccanen, neɣ la yekkat walbeɛḍ seg‑sen agemmaḍ, fhem belli lmir n lewḥuc, bab n tmurt, yella dit twanaṭ nni.

Translation.Title: The Illness of the Lion
Paragraphs: For a certain time, the lion acted as though the matter were entirely finished, and he no longer paid any mind to the wolf. He did not look for him, nor did he ask about him at all. He wanted to strike him when he felt safe.
When he judged that enough time had passed for it to be forgotten, he brought a great illness upon himself, trembling and groaning.

He sent word to the animals to come, so they could see one another and forgive each other. The animals believed it: they came. Whoever entered his cave to see him, he ate them; whoever entered his cave to see him, he ate them! Not even a single one came out safe and sound!

The wolf came as well. He called out to him from outside, saying to him:
— O king of animals, how are you?

The lion recognized him, opened his eyes, and found him far away. He turned back to weeping as if the bringer of justice had reached him:
— Come in, Mḥemmed, so we may forgive each other! As for me, my soul is departing!

The wolf refused, replying to him:
— Let us forgive each other only from right here. I am in a hurry: I have work to do!

When the lion pressed him further, he said to him:
— I find only the tracks of going down; as for tracks of returning, there are none!

The lion thundered like a storm cloud, saying to him:
— May God curse you, you traitor! O devil who broke the covenants of God! May God place the sin of all those you brought to market—until I killed them—hanging from your neck alone on the day of reckoning and punishment! From this day forward, between me and you, enmity is established; from this day forward, between my children and your children, enmity is established until the world is destroyed!
After that, each one went his own way.
Even to this day, enmity remains established between lions and wolves.

When it catches you at night in the wilderness, and the wolves are calling out or raising a racket together, understand that the master of courage is nowhere in that land; if the world falls silent and the wolves do not call out, or if just one of them barks from the opposite ridge, understand that the king of animals, the master of the land, is present in that vicinity.
Tamacahut n wuccen d inisi
The Tale of the Wolf and the Hedgehog

Source.Title: Di tebḥirt
Paragraphs: Iṛuḥ wuccen, bu meyya tḥila, yecrek taxxamt d inisi, bu yiwet n tḥilett yettsellik yess iman‑is, d nnefṣ ireṭṭel‑it i yemdukal‑is.
Assenni, ṛuḥen ad d‑akren tibḥirt ssarmen, deg‑s ayen d‑yettkatab Ṛebbi. Bab‑is yerẓa‑tt, yules‑itt, izebbel‑itt, yeẓẓa‑tt, iḥemmeṛ‑itt, yessew‑itt; yenneḍ‑as ẓẓerb ur as‑yeṭṭilli ara wuccen.
Ufan tawwurt ger tgusa, kecemen. Ččan s tawant taxsayt, afeqqus, llubyan, ṭumaṭic sxelḍen s ifelfel d lebṣel d ticcert d leḥbeq.

Inisi yellan d akeyyas, mi yečča cwiṭ iṛuḥ iqiss iman‑is di tewwurt; uccen yečča armi yeṭṭembel. Slan i lhaffa n bab n tebḥirt iṛuḥ‑d ad yessefqed: rewlen: inisi iɛedda‑d di tewwurt: uccen ur yezmir ara: yeffeɣ‑it leɛqel. Yenna‑yas inisi:
‑ Err iman‑ik temmuteḍ!
Yekcem bab n tebḥirt, yaf‑n uccen yeẓẓel, yebzeg am uyeddid, iḥseb‑it yemmut. Yessusel, iɛewwed, yeṭṭef‑it seg uḍar, iḍegger‑it ɣer beṛṛa n tebḥirt: yerwel.
Yeqqim wergaz la yeskifif.

Translation.Title: In the Garden
Paragraphs: The wolf, master of a hundred ruses, went to share a den with the hedgehog, master of a single ruse by which he saves himself, plus a half‑ruse that he lends to his friends.

That day, they went to rob a garden they had hoped for, containing whatever God had provided in it. Its owner had broken its soil, tilled it again, fertilized it, planted it, hoed it, and watered it; he had surrounded it with a hedge so tight that a wolf could not even look through it.
They found an opening between the stakes and entered. They ate to satiety squash, cucumber, and beans, mixing tomatoes with chili pepper, onion, garlic, and basil.

The hedgehog, who was clever, after eating a little bit, went to measure himself against the opening; the wolf ate until he was bloated. They heard the footsteps of the owner of the garden coming to inspect it: they fled: the hedgehog passed through the opening: the wolf could not: he lost his mind. The hedgehog said to him:
— Pretend you are dead!

The owner of the garden entered, found the wolf stretched out, swollen like a goatskin, and thought he was dead. He spat, repeated it, grabbed him by the leg, and threw him outside the garden: he fled.
The man remained behind, throwing insults after him.

Source.Title: Di tesraft n nneɛma
Paragraphs: Tusa‑d teggara n lxṛif, wten waman, teṛwa tmurt, yewwa wakal. Yiwwass, iṛuḥ inisi d wuccen ad d‑akren yiwet n tesraft n nneɛma.

Yekkes‑as ufellaḥ aɣummu, armi i tt‑yufa teswa, iɛemmeṛ‑d irden uṛciḥen, yeǧǧa‑tt ad tekkaw. Jellben ɣer daxel, qqimen la tetten. Inisi ur yettu ara iman‑is: yečča ayen i s‑yekteb Ṛebbi, yuɣal yenna‑yas wuccen:
‑ Eg‑iyi taɛrurt ad muqleɣ wi ɣ‑d‑yettafen!
Ibedd wuccen, yuli inisi f zagur‑is d temgerṭ‑is, ineggez ɣer beṛṛa, yerwel.
Uccen, armi d imiren i yas‑tent‑iwwet waḍu: iɛecca yettneggiz iwakken ad yeffeɣ, ur yufi.
Yesla i ufellaḥ la d‑ileḥḥu: yemsex iman‑is lxuf. Yuɣal yeẓẓel, yerra iman‑is yemmut: akken yexdem di tebḥirt.

Yewweḍ‑d ufellaḥ, iwala‑t yebzeg am uyeddid, imi‑s d imeẓẓuɣen‑is ččuṛen d irden; tasraft, iɛefn‑itt irkel: iǧeɛl‑it yemmut, iwwet deg fassen‑is, isuɣ:
‑ A zzehṛ‑iw!

Yuɣal yers ɣer daxel n tesraft, iɛewwed, yessusef, yeṭṭef uccen s uceṭṭiḍ, iḍegger‑it‑id ɣer beṛṛa: yerwel!
Yeqqim wergaz, ṭṭef deg wudem‑is, tamseḍ!

Translation.Title: In the Grain Silo
Paragraphs: The end of autumn arrived, the waters fell, the earth was drenched, and the soil became ripe. One day, the hedgehog and the wolf went to steal from a grain silo.

The peasant had removed the cover, and once he found it had taken in water, he gathered the wet wheat and left the silo to dry. They jumped inside and sat eating. The hedgehog did not forget himself: he ate what God had written for him, and then he said to the wolf:
— Give me your back so I can look out for whoever might find us!
The wolf stood up, the hedgehog climbed onto his back and his neck, leaped outside, and fled.
Only then did the wind hit the wolf: he spent the evening leaping in order to escape, but he found no way.
He heard the peasant approaching: fear transformed him. Then he stretched out and made himself appear dead, just as he had done in the vegetable garden.

The peasant arrived and saw him bloated like a goatskin, his mouth and ears stuffed with wheat, and the silo completely soiled; believing him to be dead, he clapped his hands and cried out:
— Oh, my luck!

Then he stepped down into the silo, turned around, spat, grabbed the wolf with a rag, and flung him outside: he fled!
The man remained there, holding his face in utter dismay!

Source.Title: Tamsalt n leɛmeṛ
Paragraphs:
Tusa‑d ccetwa, ageffur, aḍu abruri adfel.
Yiwwass, yeddukel wuccen d inisi. Lluẓen, la ttqelliben acu ara ččen. Yekfa lexṛif nni degmi n‑yufa wuccen tazart am wakal di lqaɛa, yenna‑yas: jmeɛ lxiṛ‑im, a tameɣrust!
Tura, mi iɛedda ddaw‑as, yin'as: ɛmu‑yi‑d! Mi iwala tarbibt n waḍil di tecwawt n ttejṛa, yin'as: semmum! semmum!

Ufan iniɣen deg webrid yeɣli‑yas i walbeɛḍ imeksawen. Yenna‑yas inisi:
‑ Ad t‑nebḍu.
‑ Yenna‑yas wuccen: Ala! A win meqqren deg‑neɣ di leɛmeṛ ad t‑yečč!
‑ Yenna‑yas inisi: Melmi tluleḍ?
‑ Yenna‑yas wuccen: Asmi yerɣa lebḥeṛ (Wi d‑yecfan i wasmi yerɣa lebḥeṛ?).
‑ Yenna‑yas inisi: D nek i yas‑tt‑id‑yellfen!
Yuɣal yečča iniɣem weḥd‑s.

Kemmlen abrid, ufan aftat n tasa yeɣli‑yas i walbeɛḍ n yemsewwqen. Yenna‑yas wuccen d ablaḍ iwakken ad t‑yečč weḥd‑s. Yenna‑yas inisi:
‑ D tasa kan: ad tt‑nebḍu.
‑ Yenna‑yas wuccen: Ala! A win meẓẓiyen deg‑neɣ di leɛmeṛ ad t‑yečč,
‑ Yenna‑yas inisi: Melmi d‑tluleḍ?
‑ Yenna‑yas wuccen: iḍelli!
‑ Yenna‑yas inisi: Ṭṭef‑iyi‑n ad n‑laleɣ!
Yebda ad d‑iteffeɣ si tebḍant‑is. Yuɣal yečča daɣen tasa nni weḥd‑s. Uccen yeqqim i laẓ, yeṭṭef‑as‑tt d tuḥsift.

Translation.Title: A Question of Age
Paragraphs: Winter arrived: rain, wind, hail, and snow. One day, the wolf and the hedgehog went out together. They were hungry, searching for what they might eat. The autumn was over, during which the wolf had found figs as common as dirt on the ground and said: "Take back your bounty, O fig tree!" Now, when he passed under it, he said: "Blind me!" When he spotted a small cluster of grapes at the very top of a tree, he said: "Sour! Sour!"

They found a fresh fig on the road, dropped by some shepherds. The hedgehog said to him:
— Let us divide it.
The wolf said to him:
— No! The one of us who is older in age shall eat it!
The hedgehog said to him:
— When were you born?
The wolf said to him:
— The day the sea burned (Who remembers the day the sea burned?).
The hedgehog said to him:
— It was I who kindled it for it!
And so, he ate the fig all by himself.

They continued on their way and found a piece of liver dropped by someone returning from the market. The wolf said it was a flat stone so that he could eat it alone. The hedgehog said to him:
— It is just liver: let us divide it.
The wolf said to him:
— No! The one of us who is younger in age shall eat it!
The hedgehog said to him:
— When were you born?
The wolf said to him:
— Yesterday!
The hedgehog said to him:
— Hold me, I am about to be born!
He began to emerge from his skin. And so, he ate that liver all by himself again. The wolf remained hungry, harboring a bitter grudge against him.

Source.Title: Di tqellalt n lexliɛa
Paragraphs: Yezla yiwen n wergaz axeṛfi d ameɛluf i lɛid tameqrant. Yečč seg‑s ayen yečča netta d lwacul‑is; ayen d‑yeqqimen, icelleḥ‑it, imelleḥ‑it, fesren‑t i yiṭij. Asmi yeqqur, terra‑t tmeṭṭut di tqellalt, tesleɣ‑itt.

Yiwwass, tedla fell‑as, tufa‑t ikcem‑it buṣuf. Teddem taqellalt nni ɣer beṛṛa, tsers‑itt i yiṭij, tṛuḥ tger tissirt n wawal nettat d tǧaṛett‑is. Igubeṛ‑itt wuccen: uɣalen dduklen netta d inisi ad d‑akren lexliɛa. Uccen yettuɛi, yečča armi yeṛwa; ɣas ar inisi, irfed‑it wuccen, isers‑it zdaxel n tqellalt: yečč ula d netta ayen i yas‑yekteb Ṛebbi, lameɛna, s kra yeɛreḍ deg umeddakel‑is ad t‑id‑yessufeɣ, yugi, Yenna‑yas Si Mḥemmed:
‑ Ta di tin n yiḍelli, a Muḥend! Qqim din ar k‑id‑taf lalla‑k: inisi, deg‑s imensi!
‑ Yenna‑yas inisi: Nek, lmut mmuteɣ, lameɛna ffreɣ agerruj: qerreb‑d, ad ak‑t‑mleɣ, tferqeḍ‑t keč d warrawiw.
‑ Yenna‑yas wuccen: Anida? Anida?
‑ Yerra‑yas‑d inisi: Aha‑t! Aha‑t… ugerruj! Qerreb‑d ameẓẓuɣ‑ik!

Iqerreb‑d tameẓẓuɣt‑is wuccen: iḥuza‑tt inisi s tuɣmas‑is, iɣeẓẓa‑tt. Ineggez Si Mḥemmed ɣer deffir, yedda‑d Muḥend si tqellalt, yemneɛ. Ɣas ar tameṭṭut, seg wakken tugad ad tt‑yennaɣ wergaz, tuɣ‑itent mkemmda.

Translation.Title: In the Jar of Preserved Meat
Paragraphs: A man had slaughtered a well‑fattened lamb for the Great Eid. He and his family ate what they ate of it; what remained, he sliced, salted, and they spread it out in the sun. When it dried, the woman placed it into a clay jar and sealed it up.

One day, she looked inside it and found that moths had gotten into it. She took that jar outside, set it in the sun, and went to start a mill of words with her neighbor. The wolf was watching her: then he and the hedgehog joined together to go and steal the preserved meat. The wolf feasted first, eating until he was full; then it was the hedgehog's turn, so the wolf lifted him and placed him inside the jar. He too ate what God had written for him, but no matter how much he begged his companion to pull him out, he refused. Sir Mḥemmed said to him:
‑ This makes up for yesterday's trick, O Muḥend! Stay in there until your mistress finds you: a hedgehog makes a fine dinner!
‑ The hedgehog said to him: As for me, I am already dead, but I have hidden a treasure: come close, let me show it to you so you can divide it between yourself and my children.
‑ The wolf said to him: Where? Where?
— The hedgehog replied to him: Here it is! Here it is… the treasure! Bring your ear close!

The wolf brought his ear close: the hedgehog caught it with his teeth and bit into it. Sir Mḥemmed leaped backward, and Muḥend came out along with him from the jar, escaping safely. As for the woman, because she was so afraid her husband would beat her, she kept the whole matter hidden deep inside.

Source.Title: Di tdewwiṛt n tzizwa
Paragraphs: Yiwwass, iṛuḥ inisi d wuccen ad d‑akren tament si tdewwiṛt n tizizwa. Inisi yebna ad d‑yerr seg wuccen ttaṛ n tqellalt n lexliɛa.
Ufan‑n ad ilint meyya teɣrasin uqeccuc rsent f tqamtin, ɣumment s idilen d udellas, la therrew ddunit am temdint.

Xtaṛen yiwet n teɣrast d tameqrant ǧeɛlen‑tt teččuṛ d tament. Yuɣal yenna‑yas wuccen:
‑ Qerreb, a Muḥend: keč meẓẓiyeḍ: ur k‑id yettwali ḥed: tferseḍ‑aɣ‑d kra n tament.
Yenna‑yas inisi: A Si Mḥemmed, nek afus‑iw wezzi: ur ttuɛiɣ ara: ad qqimeɣ d aɛessas: kkes‑aɣ‑d keč kra n tḥedrin.

Yekkes wuccen s tuɣmas‑is tadimt i teɣrast, yemmeɣ s ufus‑is ɣer daxel ad d‑yefres tament. Ẓẓgent‑d deg‑sen tizizwa d igelfan: uccen la teqqsent ireggel, yettsuɣu, yettemririɣ, armi t‑rrant am uyeddid.
Inisi yerra taqerruct‑is ɣer daxel, yeṛwa taḍsa: yuɣal ar yettegliliz, ineqq tizizwa yersen fell‑as; armi yekfa, yebren fell‑asent, yečča‑tent, iṛuḥ ɣer cceɣl‑is.
Ɣas ar uccen, yeqqim geddac ur d‑yeffiɣ si lɣar‑is: issetḥa ad yemmẓer di liḥala nni: yecɛef. Seg wass nni, ur yuɣal ad as‑yendi i inisi.

Translation.Title: In the Bee Apiary
Paragraphs: One day, the hedgehog and the wolf went to steal honey from a bee apiary. The hedgehog intended to get his revenge on the wolf for the matter of the jar of preserved meat.
They found what must have been a hundred bark hives resting on logs, covered with cork and thatch, making a roaring din like a bustling city.

They chose a large hive, assuming it was filled with honey. Then the wolf said to him:
— Go near, O Muḥend: you are small: no one will see you: gather us some honey.
The hedgehog said to him:
— O Sir Mḥemmed, my hand is too short: I am not nimble enough: I will stay as a lookout: you pull out some combs for us.

The wolf pulled out the plug of the hive with his teeth and plunged his hand inside to gather the honey. The bees swarmed out upon them in massive clouds: the wolf fled as they stung him, screaming and rolling around, until they made him swell up like a goatskin.

The hedgehog tucked his head inside his shell and had his fill of laughing: then he rolled around on the ground, crushing the bees that had landed on him; when he was finished, he turned on them, ate them up, and went about his business.

As for the wolf, he stayed for many days without coming out of his cave: he was ashamed to be seen in that condition: he had learned his lesson. From that day on, he never again tried to trap the hedgehog.

Source.Title: Taseqqart n jjwaǧ
Paragraphs:
Yiwwass, yennuɣ wuccen d tɛeggalt‑is, ufrarent fell‑as wallen‑is, yebɣa ad iɛawed jjwaǧ. Icaweṛ inisi, yuɣal yesnejmeɛ‑d lewḥuc, yenna‑yasen:
‑ Ay atmaten, yessefk ad awen‑mleɣ yiwet n lɛadda texṣer, di jjwaǧ, ad tt‑nṣeggem. Acimi, d lemtel, awtul yettaɣ kan tawtult, aɣyul yettaɣ kan taɣyult, alɣem yettaɣ kan talɣemt? Annect agi, ur yelli d lḥeq wala d ṣṣwab. Yessefk‑aneɣ ad nemxalaḍ di nnesba: wa ad yawi i wa tamusni neɣ lqed neɣ lǧehd, ad tbeddel ccetla, ffɣen‑d warraw nneɣ lhan irkel, ɛedlen irkel.
Si Mḥemmed d bab n wawal: lewḥuc, yufa‑ten‑id lḥal mseɛyan: qeblen‑as lɛadda yagi tajdiṭ,

Uɣalen snejmeɛen‑d tilawin, iger‑asent inisi taseqqart. Mkul yiwen iṣaḥ‑it‑id wayen i t‑id‑iṣaḥen: uccen, tṣaḥ‑it‑id telɣemt: alɣem, tṣaḥ‑it‑id tuccent d taberkant d taqurent.
Yekker welɣem ad iberri: yenna‑yas inisi:
‑ Yezla‑k ccṛeɛ!
Yessusem, yewwi‑yas wuccen tameṭṭut; ay inisi, yerban alɣem, uccen ixten‑as.
Yefṛeḥ Si Mḥemmed s teslit agi tajdiṭ: ur teǧǧi di lqed wala di lǧehd wala di sshala; lameɛna iɛewweq di ṛṛay‑is: teɣleb‑it aṭas!

Translation.Title: The Marriage Lottery
Paragraphs:
One day, the wolf quarreled with his wife, his eyes turned away from her, and he wanted to remarry. He consulted the hedgehog, then gathered the animals and said to them:
— O brothers, it is necessary that I show you a bad custom in marriage so that we may correct it. Why, for example, does a hare marry only a female hare, a donkey marry only a female donkey, and a camel marry only a female camel? This matter is neither just nor proper. We must intermarry across lineages: one will bring to another wisdom, or stature, or strength, so the breed will change, and our children will all come out fine and completely equal.
Sir Mḥemmed was a master of speech: the animals happened to be in agreement with him, so they accepted this new custom.

Then they gathered the females together, and the hedgehog cast lots for them. Each one was allotted what fell to his share: the wolf was allotted the female camel, while the camel was allotted the female wolf, who was black and scrawny.
The camel stood up to reject this, but the hedgehog said to him:
— The law binds you!
He fell silent, and the wolf took his wife; as for the hedgehog, he cradled the camel as the wolf performed the circumcision.
Sir Mḥemmed rejoiced with this new bride: she lacked nothing in stature, strength, or gentleness; however, he was utterly perplexed in his mind: she completely oversized him!

Source.Title: Tameɣṛa n wuccen
Paragraphs: Yewqem wuccen tameɣra, ur igi taqbaylit ur d‑yeqḍi i teslit, yeǧǧa‑tt d tameɣbunt meskint: ur llin leɛṛas, ur yelli nnwal, lḥaṣul d tameɣra tamessast.

Usan‑d lewḥuc ad as‑sbarken: tteklen ad ten‑yessečč, ad d‑kksen jjekk: ula d yiwen ur as‑tebliɛ telqimt. Mi yas‑yenna walbeɛḍ: Mebṛuk tameṭṭut, a Si Mḥemmed! yerr‑as‑d: Ma tebrek! Akken armi d aneggaru.
At Ṛebbi umi ur yehwi ara jjwaǧ nni beggnen‑t‑id deg genwan: ixelṭ‑d ugeffur d yiṭij d teslit n wanẓar d waḍu d lebraq d ṛṛɛud d webruri, armi ɣilen medden ad tenger ddunit.

Uɣalen ffɣen‑d lewḥuc ɣer beṛṛa, bbehdeln uccen, la s‑qqaren:
''Ya laṭif! Ya laṭif!''
''Rwalut, rwalut!''
''Lehwa, tafukt!''
''Uccen yewwi‑d tameṭṭut!''
''Rwalut, rwalut!''
''Ur aɣ‑d‑yefki taqessult:''
''Ad as‑d‑yefk Ṛebbi taqeẓẓult!''
Uccen la ten‑id yekkat s tqeslin tilmawin yerẓa irkel ijeqduṛen‑is.
Ssyen, yelḥa d telɣemt armi d asmi yufa tɛedda‑t: yerra‑tt i tyerza: tameṭṭut n lɛali yettaɣ‑itt yir rgaz, ur as‑yessin ara leḥkaṛ‑is!

Translation.Title: The Wolf's Wedding
Paragraphs: The wolf held a wedding feast, but he neither followed Kabyle custom nor provided for the bride, leaving her as a poor, neglected soul: there were no wedding processions, there was no cooking, in short, it was a completely tasteless wedding.

The animals arrived to offer their blessings: they counted on him to feed them so they could satisfy their hunger, but not a single one of them swallowed even a single morsel. When someone said to him: Congratulations on your new wife, O Sir Mḥemmed!, he replied to them: If she kneels! And so it went until the very last guest.

The people of God, who were displeased by that marriage, showed it in the skies: rain mixed with sun, the bride of the rain appeared along with wind, lightning, thunder, and hail, until people thought the world was coming to an end.

Then the animals went outside, disgracing the wolf and chanting at him:
''O Merciful God! O Merciful God!''
''Flee, flee!''
''Rain and sun!''
''The wolf has taken a wife!''
''Flee, flee!''
''He did not give us a bowl of food:''
''May God strike him with a tumor!''
The wolf was throwing empty bowls at them, breaking all of his earthenware vessels.

From then on, he lived with the female camel until he realized she completely overpowered him: so he put her to the plow; a fine woman is often wed to a worthless man, who does not know her true worth!

Source.Title: Tafellaḥt n lleft
Paragraphs: Yecrek wuccen taffellaḥt d inisi: uccen yefka‑d talɣemt, inisi, taxxamt‑is am tṛemmant, yefka‑d zzerriɛa. Heggan‑d lmiɛun, tagersa, tazaglutt, tafekkalt d ijebdan.

Asmi wten waman imezwura, begsen ɣer tfellaḥt n lleft.
Qqnen talɣemt, zerɛen, bdan tayerza: inisi yerkeb f tsilett, uccen yeṭṭef agelzim.
Asmi tekfa tmazirt, bran, steɛfan. Lleft ye ur n‑yensi deg wakal: deg wembrid yemɣi, yejbed tamezzurt.

Ur yeqqim ara yebberber, yezzegzew am sserris. Asmi yewweḍ, yenna‑yas inisi:
‑ Ad nejmeɛ lɣella nneɣ, ad tt‑nefreq.
‑ Yenna‑yas wuccen: Ala! Ssextaṛeɣ‑k: awi ayen yellan nnig wakal neɣ ayen yellan ddaw wakal.
Tɛeǧb‑it tizzegzewt. Yenna‑yas inisi:
‑ D acu ara tawiḍ?
‑ Yerra‑yas‑d wuccen: Nnig wakal!
‑ Yenna‑yas inisi: Yirbeḥ! Tewwiḍ!
Yemmter wuccen tiwizi, temger‑as irkel ifer nni. Asmi sellaw, iḍegger‑it d aḍegger, yeffeɣ d lfareɣ. Imiren yuɣal inisi ad d‑yeqqaz di tdeggar n lleft yessawaḍ ɣer texxamt armi teččuṛ.

Translation.Title: The Turnip Field
Paragraphs: The wolf entered into a farming partnership with the hedgehog: the wolf provided the female camel, and the hedgehog, whose home was as well‑stocked as a pomegranate, provided the seed. They prepared the tools: the plowshare, the yoke, the wooden neck‑collar, and the leather harness‑straps.

When the first waters fell, they braced themselves for the cultivation of the turnips. They harnessed the camel, sowed the seed, and began plowing: the hedgehog rode upon the plow‑tail to guide it, while the wolf held the pickaxe to break the clods.
When the field was entirely worked, they unyoked and rested. The turnip seed had sworn not to spend a single night in the earth: right away, it germinated along the path and shot up into rows.

It did not delay in spreading out, turning as green as grass. When it became ripe, the hedgehog said to him:
— Let us gather our harvest and divide it.
The wolf said to him:
— No! I give you the choice: take either what is above the earth or what is below the earth.
The wolf was charmed by the green foliage. The hedgehog said to him:
— What will you take?
The wolf replied to him:
— Above the earth!
The hedgehog said to him:
— It is a deal! You have taken it!

The wolf called together a communal work‑party, and they reaped all of those leaves for him. When they dried out, he flung them entirely away, ending up completely empty‑handed. Meanwhile, the hedgehog began to dig out the turnip roots, carrying them to his home until it was stuffed full.

Source.Title: Tafellaḥt n nneɛma
Paragraphs: Kkan ayen kkan, begsen ɣer tfellaḥt n nneɛma. Gan asudu: fetlen seksu s ibawen, dehnen‑t s zzit armi yellexs; ɛerḍen‑d widen i sen‑yettilin, iḥbiben d lǧiran. Ččan armi ṛwan ɣran‑asen lfattiḥa.

Qqnen talɣemt, bdan lxedma. Mi d‑ɛellmen taferka, zerɛen‑tt d irden neɣ d timẓin. Ssyen, yiwen ad yeṭṭef lmiɛun, wayeḍ agelzim: aḍref yettabeɛ aḍref; ass yettabeɛ wayeḍ, armit tekfa taɣezzut s tyerza.

Tewweḍ‑d tefsut, ssusun tafellaḥt; yewweḍ‑d unebdu, tewwa. Ṛebbi yenna‑d anɛam: ugar lḥeb alim.
Cellfen kra d arkul, ɛerḍen‑t: ufan‑t d lɛali‑t.

Asmi teqqur, yenna‑yas inisi:
‑ Ad nejmeɛ rreẓq nneɣ qbel, ssyen ad t‑nebḍu.
‑ Yenna‑yas wuccen: Ala! Awi ayen yellan nnig wakal neɣ ayen yellan ddaw wakal.
‑ Yenna‑yas inisi: Acu ara tawiḍ?
‑ Yerra‑yas‑d wuccen: Ddaw wakal! (Yebɣa ad d‑yerr ttaṛ n tfellaḥt n lleft).
‑ Yenna‑yas inisi: Yirbeḥ! Tewwiḍ!
Yewwi‑d inisi tiwizi temger‑as tafellaḥt‑is, deg wembrid tcadd d tadliwin d irinen, tewweḍ s annar.

Yemmter wuccen tiwizi, lameɛna ur ufin ḥaca adellas d iẓuran.
Yeffeɣ‑d daɣen Si Mḥemmed d lfareɣ.

Translation.Title: The Grain Cultivation
Paragraphs: After some time passed, they braced themselves to cultivate grain. They prepared the traditional plowing feast (asudu): they rolled couscous with fava beans and coated it with oil until it was thoroughly drenched; they invited their relatives, friends, and neighbors. They ate until they were full, and then they recited the opening prayer (lfattiḥa) for them.

They harnessed the female camel and began the work. Once they marked out the field, they sowed it with wheat or barley. After that, one would hold the plow‑tail and the other the pickaxe: furrow followed furrow, day followed day, until the entire plot of land was completely plowed.

Spring arrived, and they weeded the crop; summer came, and it was ripe. God had granted abundance: more grain than straw. They plucked a few green ears and roasted them to make arkul, testing it: they found it to be excellent.

When it dried, the hedgehog said to him:
— Let us gather our provision first, and then we will divide it.
The wolf said to him:
— No! Take either what is above the earth or what is below the earth.
The hedgehog said to him:
— What will you take?
The wolf replied to him:
— Below the earth! (He wanted to get his revenge for the turnip field affair).
The hedgehog said to him:
— It is a deal! You have taken it!
The hedgehog called together a communal work‑party, and they reaped his crop for him; along the way, it was bound into handfuls and then into larger sheaves, and it reached the threshing floor.
The wolf summoned a communal work‑party as well, but they found nothing except weeds and roots. Once again, Sir Mḥemmed came out completely empty‑handed.

Source.Title: Tazzala
Paragraphs:
Ibren‑d wuccen s inisi, yenna‑yas:
‑ Ay acrik, teččiḍ lḥeq‑iw, teswiḍ tidi‑w: ad nɛiwed beṭṭu!
‑ Yenna‑yas inisi: Yirbeḥ!

Uɣalen srewten, zzazedgen s tazzert d telweḥt: tbedd tirect n nneɛma, tayeḍ ukerfa. Yenna‑yas wuccen:
Ad d‑nemzazzal si lmuḍeɛ leflani: a win d‑yewwḍen d amezwaru s annar ad yawi tafellaḥt weḥd‑s.
‑ Yenna‑yas inisi: Yirbeḥ!
Iniswen ttemcabin irkel. Yewwi‑d Muḥend kra n sin seg widen i s‑yettilin: yiwen, yefka‑t d wuccen ɣer lmuḍeɛ nni; wiyaḍ, isers‑iten deg umecwaṛ. Netta d mmis aɛnan tirect s usaku d uqerwi.

Yemzazzal‑d wuccen d umeddakel‑is. Iṛuḥ‑d Si Mḥemmed am waḍu: yeǧǧa‑t‑in; yuɣal yufa‑t‑id zdat‑s, yeǧǧa‑t‑in. Yewweḍ s annar, la yesnukkuf, yettiqi si tidi: yufa‑d inisi ɣer tirect n nneɛma, ṛwan lkil netta d mmis! La s‑yeqqar:
‑ Seṭṭac, seṭṭac, sbeɛṭac! Naqel asaku, ay aqcic!
Yeffeɣ wuccen, bu meyya tḥila, ur yewwi si tirect wala si tednect!

Translation.Title: The Race
Paragraphs:
The wolf turned to the hedgehog and said to him:
— O partner, you have eaten my share and drunk my sweat: we must divide it again!
The hedgehog said to him:
— It is a deal!

So they threshed and cleaned the crop with the winnowing fork and the wooden shovel: one pile of clean grain stood high, and another pile of chaff. The wolf said to him:
— Let us race from such‑and‑such a place: the one who arrives first at the threshing floor shall take the entire harvest for himself alone.
The hedgehog said to him:
— It is a deal!

Hedgehogs all look completely alike. Muḥend brought along a couple of his relatives: one he sent with the wolf to that starting point, and the others he stationed at intervals along the track. As for himself and his son, they stayed right by the grain pile with a large sack and a wooden measuring bucket.

The wolf ran the race against his companion. Sir Mḥemmed flew like the wind: he left him behind, but then he found another one right ahead of him and passed him again. When he finally reached the threshing floor, panting heavily and dripping with sweat, he found the hedgehog and his son right by the pile of grain, having their fill of measuring it! The father was saying to him:
— Sixteen, sixteen, seventeen! Shake the sack, my boy!
The wolf, master of a hundred tricks, walked away without taking a single grain or even a bit of chaff!

Source.Title: Tacekkukt n wudi
Paragraphs:
Yuɣ lḥal, qbel ad bdun tafellaḥt, uccen d inisi ffren tacekkukt n wudi. Mi d‑mmektin yid‑s, inin‑as: Ad nekfu lxedma, ad neḥlu fell‑as!
S kra tekka tyerza d wussay d tmegra d werwa, mi yeqqim inisi, ar deqqal, yerr awal amzun yella wi s‑d‑yessawlen:
‑ Anɛ ɛ ɛ am!

Imiren ad yeǧǧ uccen la ixeddem, ad iṛuḥ ad d‑yečč kra si tzirett nni n wudi, ad d‑yuɣal. Ma yas‑d‑yenna umeddakel‑is: D acu akka, a Muḥend? yerr‑as:
‑ Terna daɣen ɣur‑i teqcict: nga‑yas isem Mebda… Neɣ Mnaṣfa, neɣ Mmelqaɛ. Akken armi tekfa tcekkukt taseɛdit.

Asmi ɣnan, dlan fell‑as, ufan‑tt temmečč. Uccen la s‑yeqqar:
‑ A Muḥend, d keč i tt‑yeččan! Ḥaca nekni i yeẓran anida tt‑neffer!
‑ Inisi la s‑yeqqar: D keč!
Uɣalen nnan:
‑ A win yeččan udi, ad d‑yeffeɣ yess: qbel ad neṭṭes, ad nsers d tama‑tneɣ iceqfan a‑nteffeɣ deg‑sen: ad d‑iban ṣṣeḥḥ!
Xedmen akkenni, lameɛna win yeččan udi yuki: yekker deg yiḍ: ameddakel‑is yeṭṭes: yuɣal ibeddel lmuḍeɛ i iceqfan.
Azekka nni, wa yeqqar i wa: D keč! Ur tefri gar‑asen.
Iwala wuccen ulac llqeḍ di lǧeṛṛa inisi: yeṭṭaxer‑as; mkul yiwen yuɣ abrid‑is.

Translation.Title: The Jar of Butter
Paragraphs:
It so happened that before they began farming, the wolf and the hedgehog hid a jar of butter. Whenever they remembered it, they would say: "When we finish the work, we shall feast upon it!" Throughout the plowing, the weeding, the harvesting, and the threshing, the hedgehog would suddenly answer back as if someone had called out to him:
— Yes‑e‑e‑s!

Then he would leave the wolf working alone, go to eat some butter from that small clay pot, and return. If his companion asked him: What is it now, O Muḥend?, he would reply to him:
— Another baby girl has been born to me; we named her Beginning… Or Half, or Bottom. And so it went until that blessed jar was completely finished.

When they were done with the work, they went to check on it and found it had been eaten. The wolf said to him:
— O Muḥend, it was you who ate it! Only the two of us knew where we hid it!
The hedgehog kept saying to him:
— It was you!
Then they said:
— The one who ate the butter, it shall pass through him: before we sleep, we will place clay shards next to us to relieve ourselves into them, and the truth will be revealed!
They did exactly that, but the one who had eaten the butter was alert: he got up in the middle of the night while his companion was fast asleep and switched the positions of the shards.
The next morning, each one kept saying to the other: "It was you!" The matter could not be settled between them.
The wolf realized there was no profit left to gather from tracking the hedgehog: he distanced himself from him, and each one went his own way.

Source.Title: Argaz d wezrem
Paragraphs:
Yiwet n tṣebḥit, deg usemmiḍ la igezzem am lemqes, yeffeɣ wergaz ɣer lexla, Yufa‑n azrem deg webrid yerẓa‑t wegris. Iɣaḍ‑it. Irfed‑it, yerra‑t s aqelmun‑is. Akken d‑yecreq yiṭij, teḥma tmurt, yetḥaya‑d wezrem, yenneḍ‑as i yiri, ixneq‑it: ffɣent‑d wallen‑is. Yenna‑yas wergaz:
‑ Dɛeɣ‑k s Ṛebbi, a lxelq agi, ma ur iyi‑tqaleḍ! Ufiɣ‑k‑id yerẓa‑k wegris, ad k‑ineɣ: sellkeɣ‑k si lmut: d lxiṛ i k‑xedmeɣ.

Yerra‑yas‑d wezrem:
‑ Anida yella lxiṛ i yi‑txedmeḍ? Ffɣeɣ‑d seg wemruj‑iw n ddheb d lfeṭṭa, ad iyi‑iwet wegris, iɛiwed‑iyi yiṭij, iwakken ad sneṣleɣ taslest‑iw, keč tewwiḍ‑iyi‑d! Amek ara afeɣ taxxamt‑iw: tseɛreqḍ‑iyi‑tt! Tewwiḍ‑d lmut: cehhed: ad temmteḍ!

Yenna‑yas wergaz:
‑ Dɛaɣ‑k s Ṛebbi, ma ur iyi‑tefkiḍ ccṛeɛ.
Yefka‑yas‑t. Ṛuḥen s uccen, ḥkan‑as, yenna‑yasen:
‑ Ur ssineɣ i tigi: ṛuḥet s inisi.

Akken wwḍen, yemmuqel‑d deg‑sen, yefhem ddeɛwa‑nsen. Kkren ad ṣellin, yenna‑yasen:
‑ Ala! ccṛeɛ igenni leɛmeṛ yelli! Keč, ay azrem, ers‑d ɣer lqaɛa, qqim‑d ssya, axṣim‑ik ad yeqqim ssyen: mkul yiwen deg‑wen ad d‑icaṛeɛ, ad fruɣ gar‑awen.

Akken d‑yers wezrem ɣer lqaɛa, yendeh inisi f wergaz, yenna:
''W'iṭṭfen aḥdif yawi lḥif:''
''A wer yebḍu d uɣilif!''
Iwwet wergaz azrem, yebḍa‑t mnaṣef: yeṭṭef aẓru, inɣed‑as aqerru.

Yuɣal ibren‑d ɣer deffir, yufa‑d inisi yerwel, iwwet deg fassen‑is, isuɣ:
‑ Ah! Yemneɛ imensi iɛeggalen!
W'ittamnen bnadem, aberkan uqerru!…
Di ddunit, ayen teẓẓiḍ, ad t‑tɣellteḍ; bnadem, mi t‑teẓẓiḍ, ad k‑yeqleɛ!

Translation.Title: The Man and the Serpent
Paragraphs:
One morning, in a cold that cut like scissors, a man went out to the wilderness. He found a serpent on the path, broken by the frost. He felt pity for him. He lifted him and put him into his hood. As soon as the sun rose and the land warmed up, the serpent came back to life; he coiled around the man's neck and choked him: his eyes bulged out. The man said to him:
‑ I implore you by God, O creature, spare me! I found you broken by the frost, about to kill you: I saved you from death; it was good that I did for you.

The serpent replied to him:
‑ Where is the good that you did for me? I came out of my burrow of gold and silver so the frost would strike me and the sun would follow, so that I could strip off my old skin, and you took me away! How will I find my room: you have made me lose it! You have brought death upon yourself: say your prayers, for you shall die!

The man said to him:
‑ I implore you by God, grant me a trial.
He granted it to him. They went to the wolf, told him their story, and he said to them:
‑ I know nothing of these matters: go to the hedgehog.

As soon as they arrived, he looked at them and understood their case. They stood up to pray for judgment, but he said to them:
‑ No! A trial in the sky has never existed! You, O serpent, come down to the ground and sit here, and your opponent will sit over there: each one of you will plead his case, and I will settle it between you.

As soon as the serpent came down to the ground, the hedgehog urged the man on, saying:
''     He who holds a stick and suffers harm,''
''     may he never be free from affliction!''
The man struck the serpent and split him in half: he took a stone and crushed his head.

Then he turned back around, only to find that the hedgehog had fled. He clapped his hands in regret and shouted:
‑ Ah! The supper for my family has escaped!
He who trusts a human being, black‑headed creature!…
In this world, what you plant, you shall harvest; but a human being, when you plant him, he roots you out!
Tamacahut n wuccen d wegdi
The Tale of the Wolf and the Dog

Source.Title: Ɣef tbenɛemmett n wuccen d wegdi
Paragraphs: Di ddunit taqdimt, uccen d wuccay llan d atmaten. Yiwen, isem‑is Mḥemmed; wayeḍ, Rabeḥ, Kessen lmal weḥd‑sen: ad brun ṣṣbeḥ, ad ksen ar tameddit, ad yeṛwu lmal, ad t‑id‑irren s axxam.

Assenni, ksan lmal, tuɣal tuccag tixsi deg yefri. Tsuɣ‑d. Uccay, yufa‑t‑id lḥal yecɣel di lǧiha nniḍen: yenna‑yas wuccen:
‑ Ur ttagad!
Yers ad tt‑id‑isellek: yufa‑tt‑in tejreḥ. Yemceḥ idammen, yuɣal ikemmel‑as: yenɣa‑tt, yečča‑tt.
Tameddit, mi d‑bernen s axxam, uccay yedda‑d di tlemmast n lmal, uccen ɛezlen‑t akkin.
Yeqqim weḥd‑s di teẓgi. Ussan imezwura, yeɣli‑d fell‑as yiḍ yendem deg wayen yexdem.

Yiwwass, ibedd‑d f yiwet n tiɣilt, yessawel‑as‑d i wuccay, yenna‑yas‑d:
Amarezg‑ik, ay agdi:
La tegganeḍ ger wulli!
Yerra‑yas wuccay
Ṛuḥ ssyenni!
D leɛmal‑ik i wer nelhi:
Talli am kečč am nekkini!
Yerna‑yas:
‑ Nek yid‑k d atmaten: yiwet n tɛebbuṭ i yaɣ‑yurwen: yya, meqqar, ad nemɛahad s Ṛebbi ur nemyučč!
Yenna‑yas wuccay: ɛahdeɣ‑k s Ṛebbi ur k‑ččiɣ!
Yeḍsa fell‑as wuccen, yerra‑yas‑d:
‑ Ɛahdeɣ‑k s Ṛebbi ar anga k‑ufiɣ, ard ad k‑ččeɣ!

Ssyen, mkul yiwen yuɣ abrid‑is.
Seg wass nni ay terṣa teɛdawt gar‑asen, wala ger dderya‑nsen.

Translation.Title: On the Ancient Feud Between the Wolf and the Dog
Paragraphs: In the old world, the wolf and the hound were brothers. One was named Mḥemmed; the other, Rabeḥ. They pastured the livestock by themselves: they would let them out in the morning, pasture them until evening, and when the livestock was full, they would bring them back home.

That day, they pastured the livestock, and a ewe happened to slip into a cave. She cried out. The hound was occupied elsewhere at that moment, so the wolf said to her:
Do not fear!
He went down to rescue her, but he found her wounded. He licked the blood, and then he finished her off: he killed her and ate her.
In the evening, when they returned home, the hound walked in the middle of the livestock, while the wolf was isolated far away.
He remained alone in the forest. During the first days, night fell upon him as he regretted what he had done.

One day, he stood upon a ridge, called out to the hound, and said to him:
Blessed are you, oh dog:
Sleeping in the midst of the sheep!
The hound answered him:
Go away from there!
It is your actions that are not good:
Otherwise, you would be just like me!
He added:
‑ You and I are brothers: the same belly gave birth to us: come, at least, let us swear by God not to eat one another!
The hound said to him: I swear to you by God that I will not eat you!
The wolf laughed at him and replied:
‑ I swear to you by God that wherever I find you, I will eat you!

From then on, each one took his own path.
It is from that day that the enmity was established between them, as well as between their offspring.

Source.Title: Uccen d taɣaṭ
Paragraphs:
Tenna‑yas tixsi:
‑ Ad d‑nnḍeɣ i tqejjiṛt‑iw ad ṛwuɣ.
Tenna‑yas taɣaṭ:
‑ Alamma kkiɣ‑d sebɛa tmura ara ṛwuɣ.
Yiwwass, teffeɣ si teqḍeɛt tṛuḥ, deg uzal am yiḍ ɣer rrif n wasif. Iɛedda‑d wuccen, iwala tili‑s deg waman, iɣil d nettat. Ineggez ɣer temda ad tt‑id‑yeṭṭef, yufa ulac.

Yuɣal yeffeɣ‑d, tḍehṛ‑as sufella n tneqlett, la tɣeẓẓ.
Yenna‑yas:
‑ Lḥemdu lilleh! Ɣileɣ, a weltma, tečča‑kem temda: ers‑d ad neddukel!
Terra‑yas‑d:
‑ Ugadeɣ ad iyi‑teččeḍ, a Si Mḥemmed, ɛahed‑iyi s Ṛebbi!
Iɛuhed‑itt, ters‑d dduklen.

Uccen yezwar, taɣaṭ teḍfeṛ‑it. Mi lḥan cwiṭ, ibren‑d fell‑as: yugad ad terwel. Yuɣal yenna‑yas:
‑ La d‑tesmejgareḍ tikli‑w d tqejbabin‑iw?
‑ Terra‑yas: Ad iyi‑yemneɛ Ṛebbi, a Si Mḥemmed! Ad zwireɣ.

Tuɣal tezwar, iḍfeṛ‑itt wuccen. Mi yemmuqel di lefḥul‑is la ceṭṭḥen, ar d‑yettarew yimi‑s aman. Yenna‑yas:
‑ La yi‑d‑tesɣubburreḍ! Liwelli, la yi‑d‑tesmejgareḍ tura la yi‑d‑tesɣubbureḍ: ad kem‑ččeɣ!
‑ Terra‑yas: Ad iyi‑yemneɛ Ṛebbi, a Si Mḥemmed: la yi‑d‑tettafeḍ kan tisebbiwin!
Armi i tt‑yeẓẓemlal, tenna‑yas:
‑ Ggall‑iyi, teččeḍ‑iyi!
‑ Yenna‑yas: Anida?
‑ Tenna‑yas: Di teẓrutt tamellalt.
La leḥḥun, armi wwḍen ɣer teẓrutt tamellalt, ‑ din i yettqeggil lmal, ‑ yeffeɣ‑d ɣur‑s wuccay: yerki‑t, yesxenzer‑it: yerwel. Teslek taɣaṭ tamcumt.

Translation.Title: The Wolf and the She‑Goat
Paragraphs:
The ewe said:
‑ I only need to turn around my own leg to be full.
The she‑goat said to her:
‑ Not until I cross seven countries will I be full.

One day, she left the flock and went, in the middle of the day like the dead of night, to the edge of the river. The wolf passed by and saw her reflection in the water; he thought it was really her. He leaped into the deep pool to seize her, but found nothing.

He came back out, and she appeared to him up on a fig tree, munching away.
He said to her:
‑ Praise be to God! I thought, my sister, that the deep pool had eaten you: come down so we can walk together!
She replied to him:
‑ I am afraid you will eat me, oh Sir Mḥemmed; swear to me by God!
He swore to her, and she came down to join him.

The wolf walked ahead, and the she‑goat followed him. When they had walked a little, he turned back toward her: he was afraid she would escape. Then he said to her:
‑ Are you mocking my stride and my hind legs?
‑ She replied to him: May God preserve me, oh Sir Mḥemmed! Let me go ahead.

So she went ahead, and the wolf followed her. When he stared at her hindquarters bouncing as she walked, his mouth began to water. He said to her:
‑ You are kicking up dust at me! First you were mocking me, and now you are kicking up dust at me: I am going to eat you!
‑ She answered him: May God preserve me, oh Sir Mḥemmed: you are just looking for excuses against me!
When he cornered her, she said to him:
‑ Swear to me, then eat me!
‑ He asked her: Where?
‑ She said to him: At the White Rock.

They kept walking until they reached the White Rock —the place where the livestock takes shelter from the heat— and the hound bounded out at him. He mauled him and left him looking wretched; the wolf fled. The cunning she‑goat was saved.

Source.Title: Uccen d uḥuli
Paragraphs:
Yiwwass, teksa taɣaṭ nettat d sin iɣiden, tesɛa‑ten‑id yiwen d amenzu, wayeḍ d amalas.
Ixutel‑iten‑id wuccen, yemmeɣ‑d fell‑asen. Tqubel‑it taɣaṭ s wacciwen‑is: mi d‑iqeddem s iɣiden, ad t‑tberrez, ad iwexxeṛ akkin: arraw‑is la teddun ger iḍarren‑is, la tt‑ttdarayen.

Yiwet n tikelt, ifureq‑itt umenzu seg‑sen, d aḥuli mɣint‑as‑d tacciwin: yekker‑as d wul, yebɣa ad iberrez uccen ula d neṭṭa. Akken i t‑iwwet, ifeṛṛed‑it Si Mḥemmed, idhem‑it s iɣẓer. Tetbeɛ‑it taɣat, yuzzel‑d wuccay. Lameɛna yufa‑ten‑id lḥal faten: ur ten‑lḥiqen armi n‑ufan ixneq‑it wuccen, yerna yefka‑yas kra n wuglan.

Kksen‑as‑t yemneɛ si lmut, lameɛna iẓur‑d at laxeṛt.
Yenna‑yas wuccay:
‑ I k‑yettawin, ay aḥuli, armi tettafgeḍ?

Translation.Title: The Wolf and the Young Goat
Paragraphs:
One day, the she‑goat was pasturing with her two kids, one of whom was her firstborn, and the other her youngest.
The wolf stalked them and leaped upon them. The she‑goat confronted him with her horns: whenever he advanced toward the kids, she would charge him, and he would back away; her offspring kept moving between her legs, taking shelter under her.

At one moment, the firstborn separated himself from them—he was a young goat whose little horns were just growing, and he felt brave, wanting to charge the wolf himself. As soon as he struck at him, Sir Mḥemmed cut off his retreat and drove him down into a ravine. The goat rushed after them, and the hound came running. However, they found that it was already too late: they did not reach them until they found that the wolf had throttled him and given him several bites.

They snatched him away so he escaped death, but he had looked straight into the next world.
The hound said to him:
‑ What possesses you, oh young goat, to fly so high?

Source.Title: Uccen d tixsi
Paragraphs: Yecrek wuccen tibḥirt d tixsi. Iɛuh‑d‑itt s Ṛebbi ur tt‑yečč, ur yečči leḥq‑is. Rẓan, ulsen, zerɛen llubyan. Wten waman, temɣi, tezzegzew am lebḥer.
Yewweḍ‑d unebdu, tebda la tettiwriɣ: begsen ad tt‑sswen; lameɛna teṣbeḥ‑asen‑d nnig tala, ur tt‑tuɛi ara terga: uɣalen ar tt‑sswan s ucekkuk.
Tixsi la tettagem, ifelleq wul‑is; Si Mḥemmed la yesswa, yeddekkiṛ!

Tewweḍ‑d lɣella: yella lxiṛ axlaf: lwin‑d, sseɣren, ddzen; yeqqim‑d ad ferqen. Yeddem‑d wuccen taḍellaɛt; yuɣal, mi yektal setta i yiman‑is, yektil tis sebɛa i tixsi, yin'as:
‑ Ad tt‑tawi ɛemmti, ma yehwa‑yas: nca‑lleh, ur as‑ihewwu ara!

Ur teqbil ara tixsi beṭṭu yagi: tenna‑yas:
‑ Dɛaɣ‑k s Ṛebbi, ma ur iyi‑tefkiḍ ccṛeɛ.
Yefka‑yas‑t. Ṛuḥen mcaṛaɛen ɣer lewḥuc: yenna‑yasen wuccen:
‑ Ay at leɛraḍ, amek ara d as‑fkeɣ nnefṣ talli d nek i d‑yettagmen, ifelleq wul‑iw?
‑ Tenna‑yasen: D lekdeb! D Si Mḥemmed umi n‑teslam la yeddekkiṛ: win d‑yettagmen ur yeddekkiṛ!

Inkeṛ‑itt, abaden!
Tuɣal tṛuḥ tewwi‑d uccay di teylewt, tsers‑it f ccfeṛ n wennar. Iɣil wuccen d tanalt i yellan deg‑s: iqeddem ad d‑yeddem: ḍehrent‑as wallen n wuccay la d‑reqqent si zdaxel am nazir.

Yuɣal yefka lḥeq, yerna lbaṭel: mi yektal taḍellaɛt i yiman‑is, yektil setta i tixsi, yin'as:
‑ Ɛemmti, meskint, aṭas ay teɛteb!

Translation.Title: The Wolf and the Ewe
Paragraphs: The wolf partnered with the ewe to cultivate a vegetable garden. He swore to her by God that he would not eat her, nor would he take her rightful share. They broke the ground, ploughed it again, and sowed beans. The rains fell, the crop grew, and it turned as green as the sea.

Summer arrived, and the plants began to turn yellow. They prepared to water them; however, the garden sat higher than the spring, and a trench could not reach it. Consequently, they had to water it using a pitcher.
The ewe kept fetching the water until her heart was bursting, while Sir Mḥemmed watered and sang contentedly!

The harvest season arrived, bringing an abundance of crop. They gathered it, dried it, and threshed it; all that remained was to divide it. The wolf took a large basket. After measuring out six portions for himself, he measured a seventh for the ewe, saying:
‑ My aunt can take this, if she likes: God willing, may it not satisfy her!

The ewe absolutely refused this division. She said to him:
‑ I appeal to you by God to grant me a trial.
He agreed. They went to seek judgment before the animals. The wolf said to them:
‑ Oh noble guests, how can I give half to her when I was the one fetching the water until my heart was bursting?
